title: Time Complexity Classes
description: The common time complexity classes, matched to real code, so you can recognize each growth pattern on sight.

activities.title: Does the List Have This Number?

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
You now know how to read a Big-O rating. The next skill is recognizing one on sight -- glancing at a piece of code and knowing, before you even run it, roughly how it'll behave at scale.

Some algorithms stay fast even at millions of inputs; others quietly fall apart the moment real-world data shows up. Complexity classes are how we group algorithms by that behavior -- by how their workload grows as input size grows, not by how they happen to perform on the small test case sitting in front of you right now.

subsections.title: Characteristic Shapes
subsections.content: Each class has a recognizable shape once you know to look for it -- learn to spot it directly in a loop's structure, not just in an abstract formula:
bullets: O(1) is flat.
O(log n) rises slowly.
O(n) climbs steadily.
O(n log n) curves moderately.
O(n²) shoots up steeply.
O(2^n) explodes.

sections.title: Why Complexity Classes Matter
sections.content: Two algorithms, same problem: one checks every item, the other halves the problem each step. At small n they look the same. At large n, they don't.

subsections.title: Scaling Differences
subsections.content: Searching 1 million sorted items: linear search needs up to 1 million checks, binary search needs about 20 -- 50,000x faster. At 1 billion items, linear search is hopeless; binary search still only needs ~30 steps.

subsections.title: Engineering Value
subsections.content: This is why engineers analyze complexity before scaling up, not after:
bullets: Predict scalability before input sizes get large.
Compare solutions independent of machine speed.
Cut infrastructure costs by avoiding unnecessary work.
Keep the product responsive by picking the right algorithm.

sections.title: Understanding Input Size
sections.content: Complexity classes are written in terms of `n`, the input size.

subsections.title: Defining 'n'
subsections.content: n could be array length, graph nodes, database rows, files, users -- whatever's being processed. For a matrix, n might mean rows (with n² total cells) or all cells -- always clarify which.

subsections.title: Visualizing Growth
subsections.content: As n grows, work can stay flat (O(1)), grow slowly (O(log n)), grow proportionally (O(n)), or explode (O(n²), O(2^n)). Watch how these curves separate below.

chart.title: Comparing common time complexity classes
chart.description: Small differences in growth rate become huge as input size increases.

sections.title: Constant Complexity: O(1)
sections.content: Same amount of work no matter the input size -- n=1 or n=1,000,000, doesn't matter. The best possible complexity.

subsections.title: Common Examples
subsections.content: Common O(1) operations:
bullets: Array indexing (`arr[i]`).
Stack push/pop.
Hash table lookup, on average.
Basic arithmetic and assignment.

subsections.title: The Catch: Nested Operations
subsections.content: O(1) operations still add up: put one inside an n-times loop and the whole thing becomes O(n); nest two loops and it's O(n²). The loop structure is where the real cost lives.

codeSnippets.title: Constant lookup by index
codeSnippets.code:
temperatures = [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34]

# This direct access is O(1).
today = temperatures[2]
print(today)

sections.title: Logarithmic Complexity: O(log n)
sections.content: Cuts the problem in half every step. Binary search is the classic example -- check the middle of a sorted list, discard half, repeat.

subsections.title: Halving the Problem
subsections.content: 1024 → 512 → 256 → ... → 1 is only ~10 steps. Doubling the input to 2048 adds just one more step.

subsections.title: The Sorting Prerequisite
subsections.content: Binary search needs sorted data. If you'll search repeatedly, sorting once (O(n log n)) to unlock repeated O(log n) searches is usually worth it.

subsections.title: Massive Scale Advantage
subsections.content: At n=1 million: O(log n) ≈ 20 steps, O(n) ≈ 1,000,000 steps -- a 50,000x gap.

codeSnippets.title: Binary search demonstrates O(log n)

sections.title: Linear Complexity: O(n)
sections.content: Work scales directly with n -- double the input, double the work. Linear search (check each item until found or exhausted) is the classic example.

subsections.title: Linear Patterns: Accumulation, Extrema, and Mapping
subsections.content: Most O(n) patterns visit every item once: **accumulation** (summing), **extrema tracking** (finding max/min), **conditional tracking** (filtering, e.g. evens only), and **mapping** (transforming into a new list).

subsections.title: Scale and Limitations
subsections.content: O(n) is generally fine, even at millions of items -- a modern loop over 1 million items takes a fraction of a second. Trouble comes at billions of items, or when O(n) work is nested inside another O(n) loop (→ O(n²)). Linear search: best case O(1) (target first), worst case O(n) (target last or missing).

codeSnippets.title: Linear traversal processes each item

sections.title: Linearithmic Complexity: O(n log n)
sections.content: Linear work combined with logarithmic splitting -- log n levels of division, each processing all n elements.

subsections.title: Common Algorithms
subsections.content: The go-to for scalable sorting:
bullets: Merge Sort.
Heap Sort.
Timsort (Python's built-in sort).

subsections.title: Performance Scale
subsections.content: At n=1 million: O(n) ≈ 1M ops, O(n log n) ≈ 20M ops (~20x slower than O(n)), O(n²) ≈ 1 trillion ops (~50,000x slower than O(n log n)). That gap is why O(n log n) is the standard for sorting.

codeSnippets.title: Merge sort divides and merges

sections.title: Quadratic Complexity: O(n^2)
sections.content: Every item interacts with every other item -- the classic nested loop, outer and inner both scaling with n, giving n × n work.

subsections.title: Micro-Transition: Stepping Into Nested Loops
subsections.content: Master single O(n) loops (search, copy) first -- then combine two of them and watch the cost multiply to n × n.

subsections.title: The Nested Loop Problem
subsections.content: n=10 → ~100 ops (fine). n=1,000 → ~1M ops (noticeable). n=10,000 → ~100M ops (slow). n=100,000 → ~10 billion ops (unusable).

subsections.title: Common Algorithms
subsections.content: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, worst-case Insertion Sort -- good for learning, rarely used in production since O(n log n) sorts are far faster.

subsections.title: Optimization Strategies
subsections.content: Spot nested loops that both depend on n and look for a way out: a hash set/dict can replace an inner O(n) loop with O(1) average lookups, or sort first (O(n log n)) and scan linearly.

codeSnippets.title: Bubble-sort-style nested loops

sections.title: Exponential Complexity: O(2^n)
sections.content: Workload doubles with every extra input. Small increases in n cause enormous jumps in runtime.

subsections.title: Explosive Growth
subsections.content: n=30 → ~1 billion ops (borderline). n=50 → ~1 quadrillion ops (impossible).

subsections.title: The Fibonacci Example
subsections.content: Naive recursive Fibonacci calls itself twice per call, forming a binary tree of calls. fib(40) can take seconds to minutes; fib(50) can take hours to days.

subsections.title: Optimization Strategies
subsections.content: Exponential algorithms almost always need one of these:
bullets: **Memoization:** caches results -- drops naive Fibonacci from O(2^n) to O(n).
**Dynamic programming:** solves each subproblem once.
**Pruning:** cuts branches that can't lead anywhere useful.
**Iteration:** the iterative Fibonacci is O(n) time, O(1) space -- proof that exponential is rarely the only option.

sections.title: Optimizing Space & Time
sections.content: A few patterns come up constantly when converting a slow first draft into a fast one.

subsections.title: The Two-Pointer Trick
subsections.content: Two index trackers -- `left` starting at 0, `right` at the last index -- move toward the center, swapping in place. Reverses a list or finds matching pairs without allocating a new array, keeping Space at O(1).

subsections.title: Hash Sets
subsections.content: Checking for duplicates with a nested loop is O(n²). A Set rejects duplicates and looks up items in O(1) -- add items as you go and check membership, dropping to O(n) overall.

subsections.title: Mathematical Series Optimization
subsections.content: Summing a sequence with a loop is O(n). Gauss's formula `n * (n + 1) / 2` gets the same answer in O(1). Swapping a loop for a closed-form formula is a classic optimization.

sections.title: Comparing Common Complexity Classes
sections.content: At scale, growth rate matters far more than small constant-factor differences. An algorithm 10x slower at n=100 can be 1,000x *faster* at n=10,000 if its growth rate is better. Design for the data size you'll actually see in production.

subsections.title: Efficiency Tiers
subsections.content: Quick reference:
bullets: O(1) -- constant, excellent scalability.
O(log n) -- grows very slowly, excellent for large sorted data.
O(n) -- grows steadily, fine when every item must be touched.
O(n log n) -- grows moderately, the standard for efficient sorting.
O(n²) -- grows fast, poor at scale (n=10,000 → 100M ops vs ~132,000 for O(n log n)).
O(2^n) -- explodes, impractical past n≈30.

subsections.title: Misconception: More lines of code means worse complexity
subsections.content: Complexity comes from loop structure and recursion, not line count. A 10-line function can be O(n²); a 100-line one can be O(log n).

subsections.title: Misconception: All nested loops are O(n squared)
subsections.content: Not always -- an outer loop of n with an inner loop of log n gives O(n log n), not O(n²).

subsections.title: Misconception: O(log n) means no real work
subsections.content: At n=1 million, log₂n ≈ 20 -- small, but not zero. It scales beautifully; it isn't free.

subsections.title: Misconception: Single Blocks always mean O(1) time
subsections.content: Blocks like "Find item in Array" or "List Count" hide an internal O(n) loop. Drop one inside a For loop and you've silently built an O(n²) bottleneck.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Complexity classes describe how work grows, not how many lines you wrote.
Efficient algorithms scale better for large inputs.
O(log n) and O(n log n) are workhorses in production systems.
O(n²) and O(2^n) get expensive fast.
Complexity analysis is how you choose a practical implementation.
